summary: The video presents a field-to-processor workflow from a New Zealand shoot (notably Cascade Creek, Milford Sound, and Lake Manipori) focused on extracting dramatic light from high-contrast scenes and translating it into post-processing in Photoshop and Camera Raw. The presenter walks through exposure decisions in bright sun, highlighting how much of the sky can be recovered and how to use highlight alerts and a ~3-stop dynamic-range ceiling at ISO 100 to protect shadows. The tutorial then covers practical cleanup (lens flare removal, artifact removal), selective color work to separate and enrich wildflower tones, and painting luminosity into distant meadows. It demonstrates constructing sunbeams with diffusion techniques, color grading with sky-to-foreground coherence, and careful remixes by history brush. The discussion extends to panoramic stitching and the wind-induced limitation on focus stacking, with rationale for cropping to gain depth of field in windy environments. Throughout, the speaker emphasizes keeping artistic intention in mind—drawing the eye to light, preserving color relationships, and balancing foreground and background through layered edits.

sections.description: The speaker analyzes Cascade Creek exposure, noting recoverable highlight detail and the need to protect shadows by pushing exposure after dropping highlights. They reference using camera highlight alerts to gauge blowout and emphasize maintaining a sun glow rather than harsh sun edges.

sections.description: The tutorial covers creating sunbeams with diffusion and edge-aware painting, then proceeds to color-grade the sky to complement the foreground (with a remix approach). It also discusses panorama attempts, highlighting the difficulty of matching exposures and the complexity of stitching multiple telephoto frames.
